newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel relaxes foreign currency controls.
newsitem.headline: Israel relaxes foreign currency controls.

text.p: The Bank of Israel said on Monday it had raised the ceiling on foreign investment by Israeli institutions as part of a package of foreign currency liberalisations.

Under the new rules, provident funds will be able to invest up to five percent of their assets abroad, up from a previous limit of two percent. All mutual funds, and not just those specialising in foreign securities, will be able to invest up to half their assets overseas, up from 10 percent.
Mutual funds are liable for capital gains tax on Israeli and overseas investments. Provident funds, which are long-term savings schemes, are exempt from tax on local gains.

In addition, the central bank said Israeli institutions would from now on be permitted to trade securities directly through foreign brokers. Until now, they were required to trade through authorised Israeli dealers.
The new rules regarding institutions must still be approved by capital market regulatory authorities in the Treasury.

The rules are part of a package of currency liberalisations approved in principle a month ago by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel and then Finance Minister Dan Meridor.

"These steps constitute another phase in the continued opening of the Israeli financial markets to competition and integration with money and financial markets overseas," the Bank of Israel said in a statement.

The central bank said Israeli companies would now be permitted to hold foreign securities and currency derived from foreign earnings equal to up to 15 percent of their annual sales or 25 percent of their equity.
Until now, the ceiling was five and 10 percent, respectively. The changes are effective immediately.

Israeli will also be permitted to trade in foreign futures, forwards and options for any and all purposes including commodities futures. The bank said these transactions could be conducted through foreign brokers, not just through Israeli dealers.
Until now futures contracts could only be used to cover foreign trade risks. The changes are effective immediately.

Israeli individuals and companies will be allowed to transfer up to $10,000 annually overseas or to a foreign resident based in Israel. Until now the ceiling on transfers abroad was $2,000 and to foreign residents up to $500. - Tel Aviv newsroom, 972-2-537-2211 x238
